title: Adjectives, Adverbs and Modifiers
summary: Choosing between an adjective and an adverb, the degrees of comparison and their traps, the order adjectives take before a noun, and how to spot and repair a misplaced or dangling modifier.
learningObjectives: Decide whether a slot needs an adjective or an adverb, including after linking verbs.
Form and use the comparative and superlative correctly, avoiding double comparatives.
Place a describing phrase next to the word it modifies.
Identify a dangling modifier and rewrite the sentence to fix it.

sources.title: English Grammar/Basic Parts of Speech/Adjectives

blocks.title: Adjective or adverb in this slot?
blocks.markdown:
An **adjective** describes a noun or pronoun; an **adverb** modifies a verb, an adjective or another adverb.

- After an action verb, use the adverb: *She answered the query promptly*, not *prompt*.
- After a **linking verb** (*be*, *seem*, *appear*, *become*, *feel*, *look*, *sound*, *taste*, *smell*), use the adjective, because it describes the subject: *The statement is accurate*, *The tea tastes bitter*.
- Some verbs are both. *He looked careful* (he seemed careful) versus *He looked carefully* (he examined it with care).
- *Good* is the adjective, *well* the adverb — except *well* meaning "in good health".
- Watch words that are already adverbs without -ly: *fast*, *hard*, *late*, *early*, *daily*; and -ly words that are adjectives: *friendly*, *lonely*, *lively*, *costly*.

blocks.title: Degrees of comparison
blocks.markdown:
- **Positive** (tall), **comparative** (taller / more careful, for two things), **superlative** (tallest / most careful, for three or more).
- Short words add *-er* / *-est*; longer words take *more* / *most*. Never both: *more easier* and *most fastest* are wrong.
- Irregular: good/better/best, bad/worse/worst, little/less/least, many or much/more/most, far/farther or further/farthest or furthest.
- Use *than* with the comparative (*larger than*), and *the* with the superlative (*the largest*).
- Some adjectives have no degrees because they are absolute: *unique*, *perfect*, *complete*, *empty*, *equal*. Prefer *more nearly unique* to *more unique*.
- "Any other" in comparisons: *This branch handles more footfall than any other branch in the district* — not *than any branch*, which would include itself.

blocks.title: Order of adjectives before a noun
blocks.markdown:
When several adjectives sit before a noun, English fixes their order: **opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose**, then the noun.

*a useful small old rectangular grey steel filing cabinet* sounds right; reordering it sounds wrong.

A related point: use a comma between adjectives only when they are **coordinate** — you could swap them or insert *and* (*a clear, concise circular*). Do not put a comma between adjectives of different types (*a large steel cabinet*).

blocks.title: Misplaced modifiers
blocks.markdown:
A modifier belongs **next to the word it describes**. When it drifts, it attaches to the wrong word.

- *The officer explained the new rule to the recruits in a stern tone.* — does the stern tone belong to the rule or the explaining? Move it: *In a stern tone, the officer explained the new rule to the recruits.*
- **Limiting words** — *only*, *just*, *even*, *almost*, *nearly* — change the meaning by position. *Only the manager signed two forms* / *The manager only signed two forms* / *The manager signed only two forms* all mean different things. Put *only* right before what it limits.
- **Squinting modifier:** one that could look both ways. *Staff who complete the module quickly earn a bonus* — quickly complete, or quickly earn? Reposition it.

blocks.title: Dangling modifiers
blocks.markdown:
A **dangling modifier** is an opening phrase whose implied subject is missing from the main clause, so it grabs the nearest noun instead.

- *Walking into the vault, the lights were off.* — the lights were not walking. Fix by naming the doer: *Walking into the vault, she found the lights off.*
- *Being a public holiday, the branch kept a skeleton staff.* — the branch is not the holiday. Fix: *Since it was a public holiday, the branch kept a skeleton staff.*
- *To open an account, valid ID is required.* — ID does not open an account. Fix: *To open an account, you need valid ID.*

The test: after the opening phrase, the very next noun should be the one doing the action in that phrase.

blocks.title: Worked example: fix the modifier errors
blocks.markdown:
**1.** *After reviewing the file for an hour, the discrepancy was finally spotted by the trainee.*

The opening phrase implies the trainee did the reviewing, but the main-clause subject is *the discrepancy*. Rewrite so the trainee comes right after: **"After reviewing the file for an hour, the trainee finally spotted the discrepancy."**

**2.** *The branch manager said on Monday she would announce the results.*

"On Monday" could modify *said* or *announce*. If the announcement is on Monday, move it: **"The branch manager said she would announce the results on Monday."** If the statement was made on Monday, front it: *On Monday, the branch manager said she would announce the results.*
searchKeywords: fix dangling modifier trainee spotted the discrepancy

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.markdown:
- **Adverb for adjective after a linking verb:** *The proposal sounds interestingly* should be *interesting*.
- **Double comparative or superlative:** *more better*, *most easiest*.
- **Comparative for three or more, or superlative for two:** use the comparative for two things, the superlative for three or more.
- **"Than any" instead of "than any other"** when the subject is part of the group.
- **Leaving *only* in the wrong place.**
- **An opening -ing or to- phrase whose doer is not the next noun** (dangling modifier).
- **Comparing incomparable adjectives:** *more unique*, *most perfect*.

blocks.title: Quick revision
blocks.markdown:
- Adjective describes a noun; adverb modifies a verb, adjective or adverb. After a linking verb (*be*, *seem*, *feel*, *look*, *sound*, *taste*), use the adjective.
- Comparative (*-er* / *more*) for two things with *than*; superlative (*-est* / *most*) for three or more with *the*. No double forms. Use *than any other* when the subject is in the group. Some adjectives are absolute.
- Adjective order before a noun: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose. Comma only between coordinate adjectives.
- Keep a modifier next to what it describes; place *only* / *just* right before the word they limit.
- An opening phrase's implied doer must be the subject of the main clause, or it dangles.

blocks.title: Practice
blocks.markdown:
Choose or fix, with a one-line reason.

1. The customer felt (bad / badly) about the mix-up.
2. Of the two proposals, the second is (better / best).
3. This scheme is (more popular / most popular) than any other scheme in the region.
4. She wore a (silk red beautiful / beautiful red silk) scarf.
5. Fix: Having missed the deadline, the report was rejected.
6. Fix: The clerk almost processed all the cheques before lunch.
7. The new terminal runs (quicker / more quickly) than the old one.
8. Fix: Walking into the branch, the alarm was already ringing.
searchKeywords: adjectives adverbs modifiers practice questions
linking verb comparison adjective order dangling only exercises

flashcards.front: "The customer felt (bad / badly)." Which, and why?
flashcards.back: "bad" — "feel" here is a linking verb describing the subject's state, so it takes an adjective. "felt badly" would mean a poor sense of touch.
flashcards.explanation: After be, seem, feel, look, sound, taste → adjective.

flashcards.front: Comparative or superlative for exactly two things?
flashcards.back: Comparative ("the better of the two"). Superlative is for three or more ("the best of the five").
flashcards.explanation: Use "than" with the comparative, "the" with the superlative.

flashcards.front: Fix: "This branch handles more footfall than any branch in the district."
flashcards.back: "…than any other branch". Without "other", the branch is compared with itself.
flashcards.explanation: Needed only when the subject belongs to the group.

flashcards.front: In what order do adjectives go before a noun?
flashcards.back: Opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose — then the noun. "a useful small old grey steel cabinet".

flashcards.front: Do these mean the same: "The manager only signed two forms" and "The manager signed only two forms"?
flashcards.back: No. Put "only" right before the word it limits. The first hints she did nothing but sign; the second limits the count to two.
flashcards.explanation: Same for just, even, almost, nearly.

flashcards.front: Test for a dangling modifier in an opening phrase?
flashcards.back: The noun immediately after the phrase must be the one performing the action in the phrase. "Walking into the vault, the lights were off" fails — lights don't walk.
flashcards.explanation: Fix by naming the doer as the main-clause subject.

flashcards.front: What is wrong with "more easier" and "most fastest"?
flashcards.back: Double comparison. Use either the -er/-est ending or more/most, never both: "easier", "fastest".
flashcards.explanation: Short words take the ending; longer words take more/most.
